title: Cellular test for a natural categorical equivalence of simplicial-set functors
statement: Use simplicial sets, quasicategories and internal functor categories in a fixed universe as in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones]. A degreewise injective map is a simplicial map whose map in every simplicial degree is injective. Call a simplicial map $u:X\to Y$ a categorical equivalence if, for every quasicategory $\mathcal E$ in a sufficiently large universe, precomposition $\operatorname{Fun}(Y,\mathcal E)\to\operatorname{Fun}(X,\mathcal E)$ is an equivalence of quasicategories. Let $P,Q:\mathrm{sSet}\to\mathrm{sSet}$ be ordinary functors and $\eta:P\Rightarrow Q$ an ordinary natural transformation. Assume that both functors preserve degreewise injective maps and all small connected colimits: for every nonempty small indexing category whose underlying undirected graph is connected, the canonical maps from the colimits of $P$ and $Q$ applied to its diagrams to $P$ and $Q$ of their colimits are isomorphisms. If $\eta_{\varnothing}$ and $\eta_{\Delta^n}$ for every integer $n\geq0$ are categorical equivalences, then $\eta_K$ is a categorical equivalence for every small simplicial set $K$.

source.place: Agent-formulated general cellular criterion underlying the proof of Proposition 4.2.3; Corollary 1.3.10 and Corollaries 2.3.16, 2.3.18, 2.3.29 in the Joyal model structure. Read online, revision July 30, 2026. No Stacks tag states this quasicategorical result; WANTED: archived source.

proof.text: Work in the Joyal model structure of [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure]. Every simplicial set is cofibrant, since its map from the empty simplicial set is degreewise injective. By [lem-coef-joyal-functor-equivalence-test], the categorical equivalences specified in the item are exactly the weak equivalences of this model structure. Call $L$ good when $\eta_L$ is such a weak equivalence. The hypotheses give goodness of the empty simplicial set and of every standard simplex. Goodness is invariant under a simplicial isomorphism $a:L\cong L\prime$: naturality expresses $\eta_{L\prime}=Q(a)\eta_LP(a)^{-1}$, and isomorphisms and composites of weak equivalences are weak equivalences.

source.place: Theorem 3.6.8; Definition 3.3.7 and Theorem 3.6.1; preparation for Proposition 4.2.3

proof.text: For a map $f:S\to T$ of spans $S=(X\leftarrow A\hookrightarrow B)$ and $T=(X\prime\leftarrow A\prime\hookrightarrow B\prime)$ whose three components are Joyal weak equivalences, use [lem-coef-reedy-model-structure] on the three-object category with $A\to X$ inverse, $A\to B$ direct, and degrees $d(X)=0,d(A)=1,d(B)=2$. The only nonidentity arrows are these two, so their inverse-then-direct factorizations are unique. Latching objects are empty at $X,A$ and equal to $A$ at $B$; the only nonterminal matching object is $X$ at $A$. Consequently $S,T$ are Reedy cofibrant: their initial maps at $X,A$ are monomorphisms, and their relative maps at $B$ are the assumed monomorphisms $A\hookrightarrow B$ and $A\prime\hookrightarrow B\prime$. The Reedy weak equivalences are retract closed by the Reedy node, and the Reedy cofibrations and fibrations are retract closed by [lem-coef-lifting-class-closure], since each is the lifting class of the other weak factorization system; so Brown's hypotheses hold. Apply [lem-coef-brown-split-factorizations] in this Reedy model category to obtain span maps $S\xrightarrow{i}R\xrightarrow{p}T$ and $s:T\to R$, with $pi=f$, $ps=1_T$, $i,s$ Reedy cofibrations and $p$ a Reedy trivial fibration. This is precisely the three-degree construction: factor $X\amalg X\prime\to X\prime$, then $A\amalg A\prime\to A\prime\times_{X\prime}R_X$, then $(B\amalg B\prime)\amalg_{A\amalg A\prime}R_A\to B\prime$ as cofibrations followed by trivial fibrations in the relative matching objects. The partial-factorization clause of the Reedy node supplies the compatibility of the three factorizations.

source.place: Theorem 5.2.5 and Lemma 5.2.6, printed pp.125-127: the mixed Reedy structure on a span and its degreewise factorization; Brown split factorization as in the pinned Mathlib BrownLemma source.

proof.text:
The Reedy weak equivalences are objectwise by [lem-coef-reedy-model-structure]. Thus $p$ and $f$ are weak equivalences there, and $pi=f$, $ps=1_T$ make $i,s$ weak equivalences by two-out-of-three. They are therefore Reedy trivial cofibrations. For either $t:U\to R$ equal to $i$ or $s$, the trivial-cofibration characterization in the same node gives trivial cofibrations $t_X:U_X\to R_X$ and $k_t:U_B\amalg_{U_A}R_A\to R_B$. The induced map on span pushouts factors as
$$U_X\amalg_{U_A}U_B\longrightarrow R_X\amalg_{U_A}U_B\cong R_X\amalg_{R_A}(R_A\amalg_{U_A}U_B)\longrightarrow R_X\amalg_{R_A}R_B.$$
The first arrow is a pushout of $t_X$, and the last is a pushout of $k_t$. The middle isomorphism holds because maps out of either object are exactly a map from $R_X$ and a map from $U_B$ agreeing on $U_A$; the map from $R_A$ on the right is forced by $R_A\to R_X$. Trivial cofibrations are the left lifting class against fibrations by [lem-coef-joyal-model-structure], so [lem-coef-lifting-class-closure] makes both displayed arrows trivial cofibrations and their composite a weak equivalence. This proves that the pushout maps induced by $i,s$ are weak equivalences.

source.place: Theorem 5.2.5 and Lemma 5.2.6, printed pp.125-127: the mixed Reedy structure on a span and its degreewise factorization; Brown split factorization as in the pinned Mathlib BrownLemma source.

proof.text: Write $|U|=U_X\amalg_{U_A}U_B$ for a span pushout. Its universal property makes these pushout maps functorial: they agree with the component maps on both summands, so $|p||s|=1_{|T|}$ and $|p||i|=|f|$. Since $|s|$ is a weak equivalence, two-out-of-three gives that $|p|$ is one, and then $|f|$ is one as well. Apply this comparison to the map of image spans induced by $\eta$ for $L=X\amalg_A B$, where $A\hookrightarrow B$ is monic and $X,A,B$ are good. The span indexing category is nonempty and connected. The hypotheses on $P,Q$ therefore identify the image-span pushouts with $P(L),Q(L)$, and their right legs are monomorphisms. Their component maps are weak equivalences by goodness. Naturality identifies the induced pushout comparison with $\eta_L$, because both have the same restrictions to the two pushout summands. Hence $L$ is good.

source.place: Theorem 5.2.5 and Lemma 5.2.6, printed pp.125-127: the mixed Reedy structure on a span and its degreewise factorization; Brown split factorization as in the pinned Mathlib BrownLemma source.

proof.text: Goodness is closed under small nonzero limit-ordinal colimits. Let $\lambda$ be a small nonzero limit ordinal and $(L_\alpha)_{\alpha<\lambda}$ a diagram of good simplicial sets. Its ordinal category is nonempty and filtered: any two indices map to their maximum, and parallel arrows in a poset are equal. It is connected for the same reason. Thus $P,Q$ preserve its colimit, and the natural transformation $(\eta_{L_\alpha})$ is an objectwise Joyal weak equivalence by goodness. Apply [lem-coef-joyal-filtered-equivalences] to these two image diagrams. It gives a weak equivalence between their colimits; the preservation isomorphisms identify it with $\eta_{\operatorname{colim}L_\alpha}$, because both maps have the same composite with every structure map by naturality. This proves goodness of the colimit. In particular it applies to continuous chains of monomorphisms and to $\lambda=\omega$. A chain with no attachment has its starting object as endpoint; successor endpoints are handled by Step 4. The cited filtered-colimit theorem does not require monomorphism transitions, so no extra preservation hypothesis is imposed on $P,Q$.

source.place: Corollary 3.9.8, printed pp. 134-135: weak categorical equivalences are stable under all small filtered colimits.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-infinity-monomorphism-boundary-cells] to $\varnothing\hookrightarrow L$ to obtain subobjects $Z_0=\varnothing\hookrightarrow Z_1\hookrightarrow\cdots$ with colimit $L$, where stage $n$ attaches the nondegenerate $n$-simplices along their boundaries. The same statement applied to $\varnothing\hookrightarrow\partial\Delta^n$ constructs that boundary using cells of dimension less than $n$: a nondegenerate simplex of $\Delta^n$ corresponds to a strictly increasing vertex map, and one belongs to the boundary exactly when its image is a proper subset of $[n]$, so its dimension is less than $n$. For $n=0$ the boundary is empty. A stage attaching a small family $(\partial\Delta^n\to\Delta^n)_{t\in T}$ to $X$ can be refined to individual attachments: well-order $T$ with order type $\tau$ and put $V_\beta=X\amalg_{\coprod_{t<\beta}\partial\Delta^n}\coprod_{t<\beta}\Delta^n$ for $\beta\leq\tau$. Maps from $V_\beta$ to any simplicial set are exactly a map from $X$ and a map from each included cell agreeing on its boundary. This describes $V_0=X$, identifies each successor as a single-cell pushout and each nonzero limit as the colimit of its predecessors, and identifies $V_\tau$ with the original simultaneous attachment. These transition maps are monomorphisms: degreewise, each new cell glues in its complement of the boundary without identifying any old elements. This refinement is a construction in simplicial sets; no preservation of these coproducts by $P$ or $Q$ is asserted.

source.place: Theorem 1.3.8 and Corollary 1.3.10; explicit refinement of each boundary-cell stage by its universal property

proof.text: Prove by induction on $n\geq0$ that every simplicial set with no nondegenerate simplices of dimension greater than $n$ is good; the starting assertion in dimension $-1$ is the empty simplicial set. Assume the assertion in all lower dimensions. Step 6 constructs $\partial\Delta^n$ in finitely many stages of cells of dimensions less than $n$. Equivalently it has dimension at most $n-1$, so the inductive hypothesis makes it good (for $n=0$ use the empty-set hypothesis). Let $L$ have dimension at most $n$. In its filtration of Step 6, the stages before the $n$-cell attachment have dimension at most $n-1$, and hence are good; let $X=Z_n$ be the last of them. Refine the $n$-cell attachment to the continuous chain $(V_\beta)_{\beta\leq\tau}$ of Step 6. Induct on $\beta$: the base $V_0=X$ is good, a successor is good by Step 4 using goodness of $\partial\Delta^n$, $\Delta^n$ and $V_\beta$, and every nonzero limit is good by Step 5. The boundary inclusions into the standard simplices are monomorphisms, as are the transition maps by Step 6; the attaching maps from boundaries to the old base need not be monomorphisms. Thus $V_\tau=Z_{n+1}$ is good. All later stages add no cells and their maps are isomorphisms, since $L$ has no higher nondegenerate simplices; their colimit is $L$. Hence $L\cong Z_{n+1}$ is good. This proves the dimension induction, including arbitrary small infinite sets of cells in each fixed dimension.

source.place: Corollary 1.3.10, expanded dimension induction using Steps 4-6; the representable hypotheses remain the hypotheses of the item

proof.text: For arbitrary small $K$, use its boundary-cell sequence $(Z_n)$ from Step 6. Each $Z_n$ has dimension less than $n$: it is assembled from simplices of dimensions $0,\ldots,n-1$, and these simplices and their degeneracies contain no higher nondegenerate simplex. Thus Step 7 makes every $Z_n$ good, including $Z_0=\varnothing$. Its transitions are monomorphisms and its colimit is $K$. Step 5 for the nonzero limit ordinal $\omega$ gives that $\eta_K$ is a Joyal weak equivalence. By [lem-coef-joyal-functor-equivalence-test], precomposition by this very map is an equivalence of the entire functor quasicategories into every quasicategory in a sufficiently large universe. This is the conclusion with exactly the categorical-equivalence convention stated in the item.

source.place: Corollary 1.3.10 and Theorem 3.6.8; conclusion of the cellular reduction underlying Proposition 4.2.3
